title: SEC standing down in RJ Luis legal battle, allowing LSU to add 2025 NBA Draft entrant to roster
content:
After months of legal back-and-forth, the SEC is finally standing down in its fight against LSU and prospective men’s basketball player RJ Luis.

According to one of Luis’ attorneys, Tony Clayton, the conference’s attorneys informed Luis’ counsel on Monday that “the SEC will abide by the terms of the preliminary injunction while it remains in place and will not impose penalties or fines on LSU if places Mr. Luis on its men’s basketball roster.”

Luis was granted a preliminary injunction by an East Baton Rouge judge on Friday, which deemed the 6-foot-7 wing eligible, forced LSU to roster him and — perhaps most importantly — prohibited “any penalty or threat” by the NCAA, SEC or commissioner Greg Sankey, according to the court filing obtained by The Athletic.

“RJ has great respect for the SEC and its member institutions, and we are all grateful to the Conference and to the Louisiana courts for working through this in an orderly legal process where everyone was heard,” Elliot Abrams, another one of Luis’ attorneys, told The Athletic. “RJ is healthy, ready, and looking forward to joining his teammates.”

The SEC had argued that Luis, the 2024-25 Big East Player of the Year, was ineligible because he signed contracts with NBA teams.

Instead, the door is now open for LSU coach Will Wade to formally add Luis to his team and to potentially play him as soon as this week. LSU, which broke into the AP poll at No. 25 on Monday, hosts Louisiana-Monroe on Wednesday.

“The SEC will of course abide by the terms of the preliminary injunction while it remains in place,” a conference spokesperson said.

Luis practiced with the Tigers early this offseason but is not currently listed on LSU’s roster.

After starring at St. John’s in 2024-25, Luis entered the 2025 NBA Draft but went unselected. He ultimately signed a two-way contract with the Utah Jazz and was later traded to the Boston Celtics but never appeared in a regular-season NBA game.

After LSU’s 81-80 win over Gonzaga on Friday night, Wade declined to comment on Luis’ situation, citing ongoing litigation. But earlier that same day, Wade testified virtually from Spokane, Wash., that the only reason he hadn’t added Luis to his roster yet was because of fear of retribution from the SEC.

Luis’ situation is just one piece of a larger legal bout between the SEC and LSU, most of which concerns the eligibility of players who previously signed professional contracts. That standoff reached a crescendo in September, after LSU football coach Lane Kiffin attempted to add two players — tight end Dae’Quan Wright and defensive tackle Zxavian Harris — who had participated in NFL training camps this summer. While a Louisiana judge ruled that Kiffin could add those players, the SEC countersued LSU, Kiffin and other school administrators in federal court, seeking a preliminary and permanent injunction that would prohibit the Tigers from playing athletes who signed NFL contracts.

Although Kiffin did not roster those players, the SEC argued last month it was like saying “someone caught with his hand in the cookie jar has cured the problem by pulling it out. What’s more, Defendants still have their hands in the jar.” The other cookie, according to the SEC’s filing? Luis.
That suit remains pending; the next procedural hearing is set for Wednesday.

Friday’s injunction, though, was the fourth consecutive court ruling that went in Luis’ favor. He previously earned an injunction against the NCAA in August, a ruling which both a Louisiana court of appeals and the state supreme court declined to stay.

LSU did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Athletic’s Matt Baker contributed reporting.
